DOCUMENT TITLE: Machine Learning Methods for Financial Fraud Detection
ABSTRACT: Machine learning techniques have substantially improved the ability to identify complex fraud patterns in financial transactions. We evaluate gradient boosting, random forests, and deep neural networks on a large transaction corpus and show that learned models detect evolving and previously unseen fraud schemes far more reliably than conventional rule-based systems, raising recall by 23 percent at a fixed false positive budget.
AUTHOR KEYWORDS: fraud detection; machine learning; financial transactions

DOCUMENT TITLE: Blockchain Adoption and Transparency in Accounting Processes
SOURCE TITLE: International Journal of Accounting Information Systems
ABSTRACT: This study examines how distributed ledger technology affects transparency in corporate accounting. Drawing on twelve organisational case studies, we find that blockchain-based recording increases auditability and reduces the opportunity for undisclosed adjustment of financial records, while imposing substantial integration costs on existing enterprise systems.

DOCUMENT TITLE: Transformer Architectures Outperform Classical Models in Text Classification
ABSTRACT: We benchmark transformer-based language models against support vector machines, naive Bayes, and gradient boosted trees across eight text classification datasets. Transformer models outperform the classical baselines on every dataset, with the largest gains on tasks requiring long-range contextual reasoning.

DOCUMENT TITLE: Class Imbalance Strategies for Transaction Anomaly Detection
ABSTRACT: Fraudulent transactions represent a tiny fraction of payment traffic, which makes anomaly detectors prone to majority-class bias. We compare resampling, cost-sensitive learning, and synthetic minority oversampling, and report that cost-sensitive objectives give the most stable precision-recall trade-off in production settings.

DOCUMENT TITLE: Explainability Requirements for Automated Credit Decisions
ABSTRACT: Regulatory frameworks increasingly require that automated credit and risk decisions be explainable to affected customers. We survey post-hoc explanation methods and argue that feature attribution alone does not satisfy contestability requirements.

DOCUMENT TITLE: Graph Neural Networks for Payment Network Analysis
ABSTRACT: Payment systems form dense transaction graphs whose structure carries signal about coordinated abuse. We apply graph neural networks to inter-account transfer graphs and detect collusive rings that node-level classifiers miss entirely.
AUTHOR KEYWORDS: graph neural networks; payment networks; collusion

DOCUMENT TITLE: A Survey of Real-Time Streaming Architectures in Banking
ABSTRACT: We survey streaming data architectures deployed by retail banks, covering ingestion, windowed aggregation, and latency budgets. The review is descriptive and does not evaluate detection accuracy of any downstream model.

DOCUMENT TITLE: Reassessing Learned Models Against Rule Engines in Card Fraud Screening
ABSTRACT: In a controlled twelve-month deployment we find no significant improvement from machine learning classifiers over a well-tuned rule engine for card fraud screening. Our result contradicts the widely reported claim that learned models identify complex fraud patterns in financial transactions more effectively, once alert-handling capacity is held constant.

DOCUMENT TITLE: Evaluation Metrics for Highly Imbalanced Binary Classification
ABSTRACT: Accuracy is misleading when the positive class is rare. We formalise the relationship between precision-recall area and cost-weighted utility, and recommend reporting partial AUC at operationally relevant false positive rates.

DOCUMENT TITLE: Concept Drift in Deployed Fraud Detection Systems
ABSTRACT: Fraud strategies change faster than model retraining cycles. We quantify performance decay in three production detectors and show that unattended models lose roughly a third of their recall within six months of deployment.
AUTHOR KEYWORDS: concept drift; model decay; fraud detection
